stem: Which building material is cheap and cool but has a short life and a high fire risk?

options.content: Thatch
Concrete blocks
Stone
options.rationale: Stone lasts a very long time and does not burn.

options.content: Corrugated iron sheets
options.rationale: Iron does not burn and is hot in the sun.

explanation: Grass thatch is cheap, local and cool but burns easily and must be replaced every few years.

stem: Why are concrete floors used in piggeries?

options.content: They are hard-wearing and easy to clean
options.rationale: Correct: pigs root and floors must be washed.

options.content: They keep the pigs warm in winter
options.rationale: Concrete is cold; bedding or heat may be needed.

options.content: They are the cheapest floor that can be laid in a pig house
They absorb urine so the pen stays dry
options.rationale: Concrete sheds urine to drains; it does not absorb it.

explanation: Concrete resists rooting and can be washed and disinfected; it is sloped to a drain.

stem: Why should a poultry house have good ventilation?

options.content: To let any predators that get in find their way out again
To make the birds lay at night
options.rationale: Ventilation does not control laying time.

options.content: To save money on the walls
To remove heat, moisture and ammonia

explanation: Fresh air removes heat, moisture, dust and ammonia from droppings, keeping birds healthy.

stem: Which property makes burnt bricks better than sun-dried earth bricks for walls?

options.content: They are cheaper to make because no fuel is needed
options.rationale: Firing uses fuel, so they cost more.

options.content: They are lighter to carry
They are eaten less by livestock and termites
They are stronger and do not erode in the rain

explanation: Firing makes bricks hard and weather-resistant, while unfired earth weakens when wet.

stem: In which direction should the long axis of a long, narrow broiler house in Zimbabwe usually run?

options.content: North to south
options.rationale: The long walls would face the morning and afternoon sun.

options.content: East to west
options.rationale: Correct: the sun then shines on the short ends, not the long walls.

options.content: It makes no difference
options.rationale: Orientation affects heat in the house.

options.content: Towards the homestead
options.rationale: Houses are placed downwind of the homestead.

explanation: Running east to west keeps direct sun off the long sides, reducing heat stress.
hints: Where does the sun rise and set?

stem: Many broilers in an overcrowded house develop breathing problems and grow slowly. Which change would help most?

options.content: Close the curtains completely to keep the house warm
Add more birds so they keep each other warm
Reduce the number of birds and improve ventilation
options.rationale: Correct: crowding raises heat, moisture and ammonia.

options.content: Remove the footbath at the door

explanation: Lower stocking density and better ventilation reduce ammonia, heat and disease.
hints: Think of space per bird and fresh air.

stem: Why is a footbath placed at the entrance of a livestock house?

options.content: To water the animals
To disinfect boots and keep out disease
To cool the air inside the house in hot weather
options.rationale: A footbath is too small to cool a house.

options.content: To wash the floor automatically
options.rationale: It does not wash the floor.

explanation: A disinfectant footbath reduces the spread of pathogens carried on boots.

stem: A farmer compares two wall materials for a store: pole and dagga costing US\$200 and lasting about 4 years, and burnt brick costing US\$1,200 and lasting about 40 years. Which statement is correct?

options.content: Pole and dagga is more cost-effective because it costs far less to build at the start
options.rationale: It costs more per year of life.

options.content: Brick costs less per year of life (US\$30) than pole and dagga (US\$50)
Both cost the same per year of life
Brick costs six times as much per year
options.rationale: It costs six times as much to build, not per year.

explanation: Pole and dagga: US\$200 ÷ 4 = US\$50 per year. Brick: US\$1,200 ÷ 40 = US\$30 per year.
hints: Divide each cost by its life.

stem: Corrugated iron sheets are fire-proof and termite-proof.
explanation: True, though they are hot in the sun, noisy in rain and rust unless galvanised or painted.

stem: The floor of a pig pen should slope away from the sleeping area towards a drain.
explanation: True. The slope carries urine and washing water away from the dry sleeping area.

stem: A wall is 6 m long and 2.5 m high, with a window 1.5 m wide and 1 m high. Assume 12.5 concrete blocks are needed per square metre. Calculate the number of blocks needed. Round UP to whole blocks.
explanation: Wall = 6 × 2.5 = 15 m²; window = 1.5 × 1 = 1.5 m²; area = 13.5 m²; blocks = 13.5 × 12.5 = 168.75, so 169. Forgetting the window gives 188.
workedSolution:
1. Wall area = 6 × 2.5 = 15 m².
2. Window area = 1.5 × 1 = 1.5 m².
3. Area to build = 15 − 1.5 = 13.5 m².
4. Blocks = 13.5 × 12.5 = 168.75, rounded up to 169.
hints: Subtract the window area from the wall area first.

stem: A broiler house measures 8 m by 5 m. Assume a stocking density of 10 broilers per square metre. How many broilers can it hold?
explanation: Floor area = 8 × 5 = 40 m²; 40 × 10 = 400 birds.

stem: A store wall is 4 m long and 3 m high with no openings. Assume 50 bricks are needed per square metre. How many bricks are needed?
explanation: Area = 4 × 3 = 12 m²; 12 × 50 = 600 bricks.

stem: Name the coating of zinc that protects corrugated iron sheets from rusting.
explanation: **Galvanising**.

stem: Explain **two** requirements of a good house for rabbits or poultry.

points.description: Requirement 1 stated (e.g. ventilation / drainage / space / security / hygiene / light).
Benefit explained (e.g. ventilation removes ammonia and heat, reducing respiratory disease).
Benefit explained (e.g. security mesh keeps out predators and thieves; enough space prevents stress and fighting).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The house needs good ventilation, which removes heat, moisture and ammonia from droppings and so reduces respiratory disease and heat stress. It must also be secure, with strong wire mesh and a lockable door, to keep out predators such as dogs and snakes and to prevent theft.

explanation: Requirement plus reason, twice.
hints: Choose two requirements and explain each benefit.

stem:
A farmer near Gweru is roofing a new pig house. He compares three roofs.

| Roof | Cost (US\$) | Expected life (years) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Thatch | 240 | 6 |
| Corrugated iron (galvanised) | 840 | 20 |
| Corrugated iron with insulation board under it | 1,260 | 30 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost per year of life of the thatch roof.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which statement about the two iron roofs is correct?

options.content: The insulated roof costs much more per year of life
The plain iron roof costs less per year than the thatch
options.rationale: Thatch is US\$40 per year, slightly less.

options.content: They cost the same per year of life, US\$42
The insulated roof is cheaper to build

parts.explanation: Plain iron: US\$840 ÷ 20 = US\$42; insulated iron: US\$1,260 ÷ 30 = US\$42.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the farmer might choose the insulated iron roof although it costs the most to build.

points.description: Insulation keeps the house cooler, reducing heat stress in pigs (which cannot sweat much).
It lasts longest, is fire-proof and needs less maintenance, at the same cost per year as plain iron.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe **three** other features the pig house should have.

points.description: Concrete floor sloping to a drain (easy cleaning, dry floor).
Separate dry sleeping area and dunging area / guard rails in farrowing pens.
Good ventilation with roof overhangs / feed trough and drinker / strong walls and gates / footbath.

explanation: Compare materials by cost per year of life, then add the animal's needs.
hints: Think about heat under an iron roof.

stem: A youth group near Masvingo has little cash but plenty of labour, and wants to build a house for 300 layers. Discuss the choice of building materials for the walls and roof.

points.description: Earth/pole and dagga or sun-dried bricks are cheap and use their labour, with good insulation, but erode, attract termites and need maintenance.
Burnt bricks or blocks are durable, fire- and termite-proof but cost more (cement, fuel).
Thatch is cheap and cool but a fire risk with a short life; iron is durable and fire-proof but hot unless insulated or high-pitched with overhangs.
Layer houses need ventilation: low walls with wire mesh above suit both cheap and costly materials.
Security against predators and theft (strong mesh, doors) is essential whichever materials are used.
Judgement: e.g. low burnt-brick walls made by the group, mesh above, iron roof with good ventilation, or cheaper local materials if cash is very short, upgraded later.

levels.descriptor: Accurate, well-developed explanation of several relevant points using correct agricultural terms, applied to the crop, animal or situation in the question, with a clear judgement where one is asked for.
Some relevant points explained, partly developed or only partly applied to the situation; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation or application.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: With little cash but much labour, the group could make sun-dried bricks or pole-and-dagga walls cheaply, and these keep the house cool, but they erode in rain, attract termites and need constant repair. Burnt bricks made by the group, or concrete blocks, last much longer and resist fire and termites, though firing needs fuel and cement must be bought. For the roof, thatch is cheap and cool but burns easily and lasts only a few years, while galvanised iron is durable and fire-proof but hot unless it has overhangs, good height and ventilation. Since layers need fresh air, only low walls are required, with wire mesh above, which cuts the cost of any material. I would recommend low burnt-brick walls made by the group, strong mesh and a galvanised iron roof with ventilation, because the lower cost per year of life and fewer losses to fire, predators and heat outweigh the higher starting cost; if money is very short, cheaper local materials can be used first and replaced later.

explanation: Balance cost, durability and the birds' needs.
hints: Weigh cost, durability, heat, fire and security.

stem: Sipho is building a layer house 6 m long and 4 m wide near Bulawayo. The walls will be 2 m high, but only the lowest 1 m will be burnt brick; above that the sides will be wire mesh with curtains. Assume 50 bricks are needed per square metre of brick wall and ignore the door.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the area of brick wall, in m².
parts.explanation: Perimeter = 2 × (6 + 4) = 20 m; brick height 1 m; area = 20 m².
parts.workedSolution: 1. Perimeter = 2 × (6 + 4) = 20 m; brick height 1 m; area = 20 m².

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of bricks needed.
parts.explanation: 20 × 50 = 1,000 bricks. Using the full 2 m wall height gives 2,000.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 20 × 50 = 1,000 bricks. Using the full 2 m wall height gives 2,000.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the upper part of the walls is wire mesh with curtains.

points.description: Mesh allows good ventilation, removing heat, moisture and ammonia while keeping predators out.
Curtains can be closed on cold or windy nights/days to prevent draughts and chilling.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe **two** features that would make the house easy to keep clean and free of disease.

points.description: Smooth concrete floor sloping to a drain, easy to wash and disinfect between flocks.
Footbath at the entrance / removable feeders and drinkers / deep litter that is replaced between flocks.

explanation: Calculate quantities from dimensions, then explain how the design meets the birds' needs.
hints: Brick wall area = perimeter × brick height.
